title: What Makes an AI Game Host Feel Alive
summary: Live Play Mobile explores how real-time voice AI and lifelike avatars are reshaping social gaming, player engagement, and human connection.
body_markdown:
‍ *"They come for the bingo but stay for the connection."*


Geremie Camara used that line to describe what Live Play Mobile learned from years of featuring live hosts in mobile games. Players can find a bingo mechanic anywhere. They return when a host knows their name, remembers their story, and makes them feel seen.


That idea framed my conversation with Geremie, co-founder of Live Play Mobile, about the company's move into AI avatars. The technology is advancing quickly, but Live Play Mobile's real asset is the hosting craft it has developed across roughly 100,000 hours of live entertainment. The team is now translating that knowledge into AI systems that can entertain, personalize, and learn at a scale human hosts cannot reach alone.


## Start with the Feeling


Live Play Mobile began with a simple combination: the pacing of a television game show, the interactivity of a mobile game, and a live host who could react to the audience in real time. The company launched its first 24-hour live bingo game in June 2020 and has since delivered roughly 100,000 hours of live entertainment. That history gives the team an unusually concrete view of what good hosting looks like.


A great host directs attention to the best parts of the experience. They welcome a new player, explain the game, remember a regular, celebrate a win, and console a loss without slowing the show down. Geremie described these as "magic moments": hearing your name and realizing that someone on the other side remembers you. That emotional response is the benchmark Live Play Mobile is now carrying into its AI-hosted games.


## AI Avatars Expand the Host Bench


Geremie views human and AI hosts as different layers of the same entertainment system. AI can run around the clock, enter a new market within minutes, speak many languages, and test dozens of ways to open or pace a show. Human hosts bring a life beyond the game, a personality players can follow, and the craft required to build durable relationships over time. Live Play Mobile expects both to contribute.


The most interesting part of that model is the learning loop between them. An AI host can test variations continuously and surface patterns that help a human host improve. Human performances, in turn, provide examples of timing, warmth, energy, and judgment for the AI system. Live Play Mobile already has years of hosting data and commercial outcomes against which to evaluate those experiments. Early avatar results have closed more of the performance gap between unhosted and human-hosted games than the team expected.


## Voice Quality Sets the Ceiling


Visual fidelity often gets most of the attention in discussions about avatars. Geremie kept returning to voice. Players may spend an hour with a host, and a flat or mechanical delivery quickly wears thin. Live Play Mobile needs a voice that can stay warm, energetic, and authentic while responding fast enough for a live game.


That creates a difficult production tradeoff. Higher-fidelity speech can sound remarkably expressive when the system has several seconds to generate it. A fast-paced game cannot pause for eight or ten seconds between turns. Live Play Mobile has built custom voice manipulation around low-latency models to recover some of that expressivity. The models will continue improving, but the lesson already applies broadly: the experience depends on how voice, language, video, and timing work together in real time.


## Keep the Heartbeat Stable


Geremie compared Agora's Conversational AI Engine to the heartbeat of the system. It keeps the sequence moving from language to voice to avatar, utterance after utterance, all day. Live Play Mobile can then focus its engineering effort on the parts that reflect its expertise: how a host reads the game, addresses players, chooses a call to action, stays on brand, and learns from the audience response.


That separation also helps with control. Game knowledge, player context, memory, hosting rules, and sensitive business logic remain within Live Play's proprietary scaffolding. The company can switch among fast-moving frontier models without handing over the tradecraft that makes its product distinctive. Geremie's advice to other builders was practical: identify the layer where your team creates defensible value, invest deeply there, and lean on proven infrastructure for the rest of the stack.


## AI Avatars Make One-to-Many Feel Personal


Live Play Mobile's next experiments stretch the idea of personalization across very different audience sizes. One avatar may host for thousands of players while still singling out one person by name. The same experience could briefly shift into a one-to-one interaction, then return to the larger show. Geremie compared the effect to being noticed from the crowd at a concert: a short acknowledgment can become the moment someone remembers.


I left our conversation thinking about the proposed handoff between a human host and an AI counterpart. A favorite host might finish a shift, introduce an AI version for the night, and return the next day already briefed on what happened. Players may love that idea or reject it; Live Play Mobile is comfortable learning either way. The tools have made experimentation dramatically faster. The companies that learn what audiences genuinely value will shape this next era of live entertainment.
